prompt: An alert outpatient sits down for a fasting chemistry panel. The requisition lists a full name and a date of birth, and the clerk has written outpatient room 4 on the folder. The patient is chatty, seated, and ready for the needle. What do you confirm before the venipuncture?

options.text: Have the patient state full name and date of birth, then match both to the order.
Treat outpatient room 4 as the second identifier and draw when it matches the folder.
Ask the clerk who called the name to confirm identity, then copy the requisition onto the labels.
Read the printed name aloud and start the draw if the patient nods without stating a birth date.

explanation: The patient must state two identifiers, usually full name and date of birth, and those words have to match the order before you draw or label. A room number is a location, not an identifier, and a nod or a coworker's word does not replace what the patient says.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a room number with a patient identifier. Outpatient room 4 is where the chair is, not a fact the patient states to prove identity.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a coworker's confirmation with the patient's own stated name and date of birth matched to the order.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a nod with an active identifier. Hearing the name and agreeing is not the same as stating the name and date of birth.

Stop until nursing replaces the wristband.
Ask the roommate to confirm the name, then collect the trough and label the tubes from the door chart.
Accept a stated first name, draw the trough, and ask nursing to add a wristband after you leave.

distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a roommate's word with a wristband. Another patient cannot replace the missing band or a stated date of birth.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses drawing first with banding later. The wristband has to be on before the collection, not added after you leave.

prompt: An adult with easy venous access needs a routine chemistry draw from the antecubital fossa. You can palpate a median cubital vein in the center, a cephalic vein toward the thumb, and a basilic vein toward the body. Which vein do you enter first?

options.text: The basilic vein, because it is usually the largest and the standard first site.
The cephalic vein, because it is better anchored than the vein in the center of the fossa.
The median cubital vein.
Whichever of the three veins lies closest to the skin, with no set order among them.

explanation: For a routine antecubital draw the median cubital vein is the first choice. It usually sits well supported in the center of the fossa. The cephalic comes next, and the basilic is last because it lies near the brachial artery and the median nerve.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the basilic vein with the first choice. The basilic is saved for last because it sits near the brachial artery and the median nerve.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the cephalic vein with the first choice. The cephalic is the usual second vein, after the median cubital.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses how close a vein looks to the skin with the selection order. Visibility does not replace the median cubital as the first site.

prompt: This morning's draw used the median cubital vein, and that site is now bruised. On the same arm a cephalic vein and a basilic vein are both easy to feel for a repeat potassium. Which site is the better second choice?

options.text: The basilic vein, because it lies farther from the brachial artery and the median nerve than the cephalic.
Either remaining vein, because the cephalic and the basilic carry the same risk of hitting an artery or a nerve.
The bruised median cubital vein, with the needle aimed just beside the bruise so you stay on the first-choice vein.
The cephalic vein.

explanation: When the median cubital vein is already used, the cephalic vein is the better second choice. The basilic vein is last of the three because it sits near the brachial artery and the median nerve, so it is not the default while the cephalic is open.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses where the basilic vein sits. It is closer to the brachial artery and the median nerve, which is why it is the last of the three.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses equal risk with the real order. The cephalic vein is preferred over the basilic once the median cubital is unavailable.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses staying on a bruised first-choice vein with picking a fresh site. A bruised median cubital is not restuck beside the bruise.

prompt: You tied a tourniquet about 3 inches above an outpatient's antecubital fossa. About 90 seconds have passed, the needle is still capped, and no tube is filling. The patient asks you to keep the band on so the visit stays short. What should you do?

options.text: Release the tourniquet and start the draw later.
Leave the tourniquet on until a vein distends, because 90 seconds is still safe for a chemistry draw.
Tighten the tourniquet another notch so the vein fills and you can stick without waiting.
Keep the tourniquet on and have the patient pump a fist until the vein is large enough to enter.

explanation: A tourniquet stays on about one minute or less. At about 90 seconds with no blood flowing, release it and begin again after the arm has rested. Leaving it on causes hemoconcentration, and adding fist pumping can raise potassium as well.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses 90 seconds with an acceptable tourniquet time. Past about one minute, with no tube filling, the tourniquet comes off.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses extra pressure with a fix for time. Tightening a tourniquet that has already been on too long does not make the specimen safer.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses fist pumping with a safe way to enlarge a vein. Pumping can raise potassium and does not justify leaving the tourniquet in place.

prompt: A patient here for a basic metabolic panel is opening and closing a fist hard while you look for an antecubital vein. The tourniquet is already on and the needle is still capped. How do you handle the fist before you stick?

options.text: Encourage harder pumping so the vein stays distended for every tube in the panel.
Stop the pumping, because it raises potassium.
Let the pumping continue, because repeated fist exercise changes glucose rather than potassium.
Have the patient keep pumping after the needle is in so the tube fills before the tourniquet comes off.

explanation: Hard fist pumping uses the forearm muscles and can raise the potassium in the specimen you are about to collect. Stop the pumping before the needle goes in. A still, closed hand may help you see a vein; repeated squeezing does not.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a fuller-looking vein with a valid potassium. Harder pumping is the motion that can raise the analyte on this panel.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses glucose with potassium. Fist pumping is a potassium problem on a basic metabolic panel, so the motion stops.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses faster filling with an acceptable draw. Pumping after the needle is in can still raise potassium and keeps the tourniquet on longer.

prompt: You are about to enter a palpable median cubital vein with a straight needle for a routine adult draw. The vein is anchored just below the site and the tourniquet has been on well under a minute. How should the needle go in?

options.text: Bevel down, at about 90 degrees, so the point punches straight through the upper wall of the vein.
Bevel up, at about 90 degrees, the usual angle for a straight needle in the antecubital fossa.
Bevel up, at about 15 to 30 degrees.
Bevel turned to the side, then moved left and right until blood flashes in the hub.

explanation: A straight needle in the antecubital fossa enters with the bevel up at about 15 to 30 degrees, while the vein is anchored. A 90-degree jab is steep enough to pass through the vein. The bevel is not turned down, and the needle is not swept sideways to hunt for blood.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a 90-degree jab with the 15-to-30-degree entry. Bevel up is right, but that steep angle tends to go through the vein.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses searching with the needle and a single controlled entry. Moving the bevel left and right is probing, which tears tissue.

prompt: A straight needle sits in the antecubital fossa, bevel up, at a shallow angle, but no blood enters the tube. The site is not swelling, and the patient denies pain shooting down the arm. What needle adjustment is appropriate?

options.text: Move the needle side to side in the tissue until the bevel finds the vein.
Pull the needle almost out of the skin and redirect it steeply along a new path without ending the attempt.
Leave the needle still and keep the tourniquet on for another full minute while you wait for flow.
Advance or withdraw the needle slightly.

explanation: No blood, with no hematoma and no nerve-type pain, calls for a small advance or a small withdrawal so the bevel can enter the lumen. Sliding the needle sideways is probing and can damage the vein. Extra tourniquet time does not create a flash.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a blind redirect under the skin with a small advance or withdrawal along the path you already chose.

prompt: Midway through a multi-tube draw, a bulge of blood rises under the skin and the patient says the arm feels tight. Flow into the attached tube has turned uneven. What do you do with this puncture?

Advance the same needle so the hematoma drains into the tube and this draw can finish.
Leave the needle in, release the tourniquet, and keep filling the remaining tubes through the swollen site.
Pull the needle back a little and probe sideways until the swelling stops and steady flow returns.

Stop, document the refusal, and tell the nurse.
Keep the needle in and explain that a partial tube cannot be used, so the draw has to be completed.
Remove the needle, discard the partial tube, and redraw the other arm at once without telling the unit.

prompt: A patient had a left mastectomy with axillary lymph nodes removed. Both arms have veins you can feel, and a routine blood count and a chemistry panel are due this morning. Which arm do you use?

A vein on the left hand, because a hand stick is allowed on the mastectomy side if you spare the fossa.
The right arm.
Either arm, because lymph-node removal limits blood-pressure cuffs and not venipuncture.

From the right hand, below the catheter, while the saline keeps running and the free arm is left unused.
From the left arm.

prompt: Halfway through a serum tube, an outpatient turns pale, says the room is spinning, and slumps sideways in the draw chair. The tube is not full, and the patient is still breathing. What do you do first?

Leave the needle in place, call for help, and lower the head while the tube continues to fill.
Have the patient lean forward with the needle still in the arm until the skin color returns.

Stop and get a more experienced collector.
Restick the same right median cubital vein with a smaller needle before you ask anyone else.
Change the chemistry panel to a finger stick so another venipuncture is unnecessary.

prompt: The last tube of a routine draw is full, the tourniquet is already off, and you have just slid the straight needle out of the arm. An open sharps container sits on the tray within reach, and gauze is on the site. What do you do with the needle?

Set it on the tray until the tubes are labeled, then recap it and discard it.
Put it straight into the sharps container.
Clip the steel off the hub and throw the plastic holder into regular trash.

prompt: During an outpatient draw, the median cubital vein slips sideways as soon as the needle touches the skin. The collector can still see the vein and has not entered it. What should the collector do before the needle advances?

Tighten the tourniquet and ask for fist pumping so the vein stops moving
Let go of the skin and insert at a steeper angle
Pull the skin taut below the site to anchor the vein

prompt: Blood is flowing steadily into a serum tube during a routine antecubital draw. One more tube remains, and the collector is about to finish and withdraw the needle. When should the tourniquet be released?

After the needle is out, with gauze on the site
After a full extra minute, still tightened as the needle comes out
After the patient leaves the chair and the arm is rechecked at the desk

distractorExplanations.c: Misreads the one-minute limit as a quota to finish. That minute is the longest the tourniquet should stay on, not a reason to leave it on through needle removal.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses tourniquet release with a later recheck. The band comes off during the draw, before the needle, not after the patient leaves the chair.

Bevel up, shallower than a straight antecubital needle
Bevel up at about 45 degrees, to cross the hand vein quickly
Bevel sideways at a 15-to-30-degree angle, with the hand hanging down

In the left upper arm, above the fistula, so the graft itself is not needled

The swollen forearm, with the tourniquet left on longer so the vein can fill
Either forearm, since a vein is visible in both
The unswollen arm, so edema is not drawn into the tube

prompt: A red-top tube for a chemistry panel has stood upright for 10 minutes. The clot is still soft and incomplete when you pick the tube up to load the centrifuge. What should you do with it?

Shake the tube vigorously until the clot looks firm, then load the centrifuge.
Pour the unclotted blood into a gold separator tube and spin that tube instead.
Wait until clotting is complete, then centrifuge.

prompt: On Monday morning you find Friday's red-top tube, drawn for a glucose, still sitting unspun on the processing counter. Nobody separated the serum, and the patient has already gone home. What should happen to this glucose?

options.text: Reject it and recollect in a gray tube
Spin the red top now and report the glucose as Friday's fasting result
Pour the blood into a lavender tube so EDTA stops the cells from using sugar
Relabel the red top as a fluoride glucose and send it on to chemistry

explanation: A red-top tube has no glycolytic inhibitor. Cells keep consuming glucose while whole blood sits, so a tube left out all weekend is not a valid glucose. Gray tubes contain fluoride, which slows that consumption. Reject this specimen and recollect rather than report the fallen value.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a late spin with a valid glucose; cells consumed glucose all weekend in a red tube that has no fluoride.

distractorExplanations.d: Confuses words written on a new label with the additive inside the tube; a red top is not a fluoride tube.

prompt: A tube collected for a cold-agglutinin titer is still warm from the patient's arm when it reaches the processing bench. The rack it was placed in is headed for the specimen refrigerator. Where does this tube belong?

Kept warm until the laboratory performs the test
On ice, using the same transport used for an ammonia specimen
In the freezer as a serum aliquot so the titer cannot drift overnight

explanation: Cold agglutinins attach to red cells when the specimen cools, and the serum titer then reads lower than the patient's level. The tube stays warm from collection through testing. The refrigerator, a bag of ice, and the freezer are the wrong conditions for this test.

distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a cold agglutinin, which must stay warm, with ammonia or lactic acid, which are carried on ice.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses keeping the specimen warm with freezing the serum; a freezer is not the condition for a cold-agglutinin titer.

prompt: An ammonia specimen reaches processing at room temperature. The courier left it loose in the transport bag, and it never sat on ice. What does processing do with this tube?

prompt: A bilirubin tube has been sitting uncapped in a tray on the windowsill, in direct sun, for about half an hour. The serum still looks clear. What should you do with this specimen?

prompt: While processing a lavender tube drawn for a CBC, you tip the tube and a solid clot slides along the plastic. Most of the blood still looks liquid. How is this specimen handled?

options.text: Reject the clotted tube for the CBC
Lift the clot out with an applicator stick and run the liquid blood that remains
Centrifuge the lavender tube and run the CBC from the plasma
Invert the tube another ten times so the clot breaks apart and redissolves

explanation: EDTA in a lavender tube is what keeps a CBC specimen liquid. A clot means the blood was not adequately anticoagulated, so cell and platelet counts from that tube are not valid. Reject it. Removing the clot, spinning the tube, or inverting it again does not make a valid whole-blood count.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses lifting out a visible clot with repairing the CBC; cells and platelets are already trapped in the clot.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a whole-blood CBC with a test run on plasma; a spun lavender tube cannot be turned back into whole blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses mixing right after the draw with dissolving a clot that has already formed in the tube.

prompt: A gold serum-separator tube went into the centrifuge about ten minutes after the draw. The gel has formed, but a fibrin strand hangs in the serum. A coworker reaches for a stick to pull the strand out. What should you do?

options.text: Pull the strand out with the stick, spin the gold tube again, and release the serum
Recollect, and let the new tube clot fully before the spin
Pour the serum into a red-top tube and treat the strand as a gel artifact
Stand this same tube for twenty more minutes, then centrifuge it again

explanation: Serum is centrifuged only after clotting is finished. An early spin leaves fibrinogen that appears as a fibrin strand, and lifting that strand out does not make the serum reliable. Recollect, allow a full clot, then spin. Extra waiting after the gel has already formed does not finish the job.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses fishing a fibrin strand out of the serum with a completed clot; the tube was spun too soon and should be recollected.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses pouring serum into a second tube with fixing an early spin; the fibrin problem travels with the serum.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses more waiting on an already spun gel tube with a proper recollect; the separator has already divided an incomplete clot.

Ask the person at the next bench to say which primary tube it matches

prompt: The screen flags a potassium as critical while the patient is still seated in the draw chair. The patient sees your expression change and asks whether the number means the kidneys are failing. How do you answer?

prompt: A coagulation test is on the order. The light-blue tube in the rack is filled only to about a quarter of the marked volume. The other tubes for the order are full. What do you do with the short blue tube?

Do not send the quarter-full tube as complete
Top it off with citrate blood poured from another patient's full blue tube
Add saline up to the fill mark so the tube looks correctly filled on the rack

explanation: A light-blue tube is made for about a 9:1 ratio of blood to sodium citrate. At a quarter of the fill volume there is too much citrate for the blood, so clotting results from that tube are not valid. Do not send it as a complete specimen, and do not top it off from another tube or with saline.

distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a tube filled to the line with saline with a proper draw; saline changes the citrate ratio and the clotting result.

prompt: Tomorrow's order is a fasting draw. The patient takes a prescribed blood-pressure tablet with breakfast and asks whether to skip that tablet so the test will count as fasting. What do you tell the patient?

options.text: Skip the tablet tomorrow, because fasting means no medicines of any kind
Take the tablet with coffee and cream, since cream does not count as food
Stop the tablet for the rest of the week so every later draw stays fasting too
Do not skip the prescribed tablet unless the order says to

explanation: Fasting means the patient has not eaten or taken a caloric drink. It does not, by itself, cancel a prescribed medicine. Unless the order says to hold the tablet, the phlebotomist does not tell the patient to skip it. Coffee with cream would also break the fast, which is a separate mistake from a medicine hold.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses fasting from food with holding every medicine; a fasting order is not a medicine hold.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a fasting draw with coffee and cream; cream breaks the fast, and that instruction still does not authorize skipping the tablet.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses one fasting draw with stopping a prescribed tablet for days; the order does not say to hold the medicine.
